set.text: When my grandmother Hana turned ninety, she called me into her bedroom and opened a wooden box I had never seen. Inside lay the family's greatest heirloom: a silver hair comb that had belonged to her own grandmother in Osaka. Next to it was a small memento from her wedding: a dried flower from her bouquet, pressed flat and wrapped in thin paper. Everyone in our family seems to revere Grandma Hana, but she has always been quiet about her past. That afternoon, though, she decided to divulge something she had kept to herself for seventy years: as a young woman, she had run away from home to study painting, against her father's wishes. Her story was so evocative that I could almost smell the paint and hear the trains. “Write it down,” she told me. “Not for me. For posterity.” So I did, and I keep the notebook beside the comb.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “revere” mean?
qs.why: The family treats her with deep respect and admiration. “Feel a little afraid of” is a near miss that a careless reader might choose.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “divulge” mean?
qs.why: She shared something she had kept to herself for seventy years, so she revealed a secret. “Hide even more carefully” is the opposite.

qs.q: Why did Hana want her story written down?
options: So that she could remember it herself
So that future generations would know it
So that it could be sold as a book
So that her father could finally read it
Because the narrator might lose the comb
To prove that she became a famous painter
qs.why: She says “Not for me. For posterity,” meaning future generations. That rules out writing it for herself, the most tempting wrong answer.

why: A flower cannot be pressed inside a train ticket; reworded the memento sentence so it is physically sensible (the train ticket also disappears, keeping the passage simple).

set.text: In a new courtroom novel, the trouble for accountant Martin Hale begins when a grand jury votes to indict him for stealing money from a children's charity. The main witness is his former assistant, who says she saw him move the funds. Hale's lawyer attacks the veracity of her story, pointing out that her dates do not match the bank records. Another witness admits that what he knows is only hearsay: a friend of a friend told him about the theft. The tension rises when the lawyer suggests that the assistant may have tried to fabricate emails to protect herself. In the end, the jury finds Hale culpable, but for a smaller crime than the one first charged. At sentencing, he asks the judge for clemency, and the judge agrees to a shorter sentence because Hale has paid back every dollar.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “veracity” mean?
options: how true or accurate it is
qs.why: The lawyer questions whether her story is true by showing that her dates do not match the bank records.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “clemency” mean?
options: mercy that makes a punishment less harsh
qs.why: He asks the judge to be merciful, and the judge gives a shorter sentence. He was already found guilty, so it is not proof of innocence.

qs.q: Why did the judge give Hale a shorter sentence?
options: Because he had paid back all the money
Because the assistant's story was false
Because the jury found him innocent
Because the evidence was only hearsay
Because the charity asked for it
qs.why: The passage says the judge agreed “because Hale has paid back every dollar.” The jury did find him guilty of a smaller crime.

why: Real published novels are titled The Ledger, so naming it and inventing its plot states a false real-world fact; the novel is now unnamed and clearly fictional. “culpable ... of a smaller crime” is unidiomatic; changed to “culpable ... for”.

set.text: Every spring, the Westbrook High debate team holds a contest open to the whole town. This year's final paired two very different speakers. Samuel Osei is a natural orator who fills the room with his deep voice and his stories. He spoke eloquently about why the town should build a new library, and several people in the audience wiped their eyes. His opponent, Grace Kim, took the other side. Her style was succinct: three points, each explained in a single clear sentence. When Samuel claimed that without a new library “our children will forget how to read,” Grace smiled and called it hyperbole; children were reading at the old library every day. “Then imagine how much they'd read in a better one,” Samuel retorted, and the crowd laughed. Through it all, both speakers showed civility, shaking hands warmly at the end. The judges called it a tie.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “succinct” mean?
qs.why: Three points, each in a single clear sentence, is a short and clear style. “Long and detailed” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “hyperbole” mean?
qs.why: Saying children “will forget how to read” makes the problem sound much bigger than it is, so Grace calls it an exaggeration.

qs.q: How were the two speakers' styles different?
options: Grace told long stories, while Samuel was brief.
Samuel was rude, while Grace was polite.
Samuel spoke quietly, while Grace shouted.
Grace made people cry, while Samuel bored them.
Samuel used stories and emotion, while Grace used short, clear points.
Both speakers used exactly the same style.
qs.why: Samuel moved people with his voice and stories; Grace gave three points in single sentences. Both were polite.

why: The card for retort is the verb, but the passage used the noun (“Samuel's quick retort”); rewritten to use the verb “retorted” in the card's sense.

set.text: Bat-Erdene grew up as a nomad in the Mongolian hinterland, far from the capital and from any paved road. Each season, his family packed their round felt tent, called a ger, and moved their sheep and horses to fresh grass. Life was austere. There was no running water, little furniture, and only a small stove against the bitter winter cold. At eighteen, he left to study engineering in the capital, Ulaanbaatar. He worked hard to assimilate into city life, learning to ride crowded buses, eat at noisy cafés, and dress like his classmates. Still, on hot summer nights in his apartment, he would yearn for the wide, quiet land and the smell of horses. Now thirty, he has a good job, but he spends his whole vacation each summer helping his parents. To do it, he must forgo trips abroad with his friends. “It's worth it,” he says.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “austere” mean?
qs.why: No running water, little furniture, and only a small stove describe a plain life without comfort. “Full of luxury” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “forgo” mean?
qs.why: Because he spends his vacation with his parents, he gives up trips abroad with friends.

qs.q: What can you infer about Bat-Erdene?
options: He dislikes the city and plans to quit his job.
His parents moved to the city with him.
He travels abroad with friends every summer.
He has adapted to city life but still feels close to his family's way of life.
He never learned how to live in the city.
qs.why: He learned city ways and has a good job, yet he longs for the land and spends every summer helping his parents.

why: “the hinterland of Mongolia” reads oddly for a landlocked country; reworded so the word clearly carries the card's sense of land far from a big city.

set.text: For the people of Port Ellis, a sudden flock of seabirds flying inland is often seen as a harbinger of a big storm. When the birds came on Thursday, fishermen pulled their boats onto the beach, and families began to fortify their homes, nailing boards over windows and piling sandbags by the doors. Forecasters warned that the winds could wreak serious damage along the coast. They were right. The night was tumultuous, with roaring wind, crashing waves, and rain so heavy that the streetlights disappeared from view. By morning, the wind had toppled dozens of trees, including the old oak in front of the school. The town came to a standstill: roads were blocked, shops were closed, and the power was out for two days. Yet no one was hurt, and by the weekend, neighbors were working side by side to clear the streets.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “harbinger” mean?
options: a sign that something is coming
qs.why: People see the birds as a sign that a storm is on its way. The birds do not cause the storm.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “standstill” mean?
options: a complete stop of all activity
qs.why: Blocked roads, closed shops, and no power mean everything in town had stopped.

options: The fishermen lost all their boats.
Most families left town for good.
Neighbors worked together to clear the streets.
qs.why: The passage ends: “no one was hurt, and by the weekend, neighbors were working side by side to clear the streets.” The tree in front of the school fell, not the building.

why: “the storm had managed to topple” wrongly gives a storm intention/effort; made the sentence natural.
